danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Dagen efter sin optagelse i Logen sad Pierre hjemme og læste en bog, idet han forsøgte at trænge ind i Firkantens betydning, hvor den ene side symboliserede Gud, en anden moralske ting, en tredje fysiske ting og den fjerde en kombination af disse. Af og til vandrede hans opmærksomhed fra bogen og Firkanten, og han skitserede i fantasien en ny livsplan. Aftenen forinden i Logen havde han hørt, at rygtet om hans duel var nået kejseren, og at det var klogest for ham at forlade Petersborg. Pierre planlagde at rejse til sine godser i syd og dér tage sig af sine livegnes velfærd. Han lagde med glæde planer for dette nye liv, da fyrst Vasilij pludselig trådte ind i stuen.

»Min kære ven, hvad har du foretaget dig i Moskva? Hvorfor har du strides med Hélène, mon cher? Du lider af en vildfarelse,« sagde fyrst Vasilij, da han kom ind. »Jeg ved alt om det, og jeg kan forsikre dig, at Hélène er lige så uskyldig over for dig, som Kristus var over for jøderne.«
Pierre ville svare, men fyrst Vasilij afbrød ham.

»Og hvorfor kom du ikke bare lige til mig som til en ven? Jeg ved alt om det og forstår det hele,« sagde han. »Du opførte dig som en mand, der sætter pris på sin ære, måske lidt for forhastet, men det skal vi ikke gå ind i. Men tænk over den stilling, du sætter hende og mig i, i selskabets og endda hoffets øjne,« tilføjede han og sænkede stemmen. »Hun bor i Moskva, og du er her. Husk, min dreng,« og han trak Pierre i armen, »det er ganske enkelt en misforståelse. Det ved du nok selv. Lad os straks skrive et brev til hende, og hun kommer hertil, og alt bliver opklaret — eller ellers, min kære dreng, lad mig sige dig, at det er højst sandsynligt, at du kommer til at lide for det.«
Fyrst Vasilij kastede et betydningsfuldt blik på Pierre.
»Jeg ved fra pålidelige kilder, at enkekejserinden nærer en levende interesse for hele denne sag. Du ved, hun er meget nådig mod Hélène.«

Pierre forsøgte adskillige gange at tale, men dels lod fyrst Vasilij ham ikke komme til orde, dels frygtede Pierre selv at begynde at tale i den tone af bestemt afvisning og uenighed, som han fast havde besluttet at svare sin svigerfar i. Desuden genlød ordene fra frimurerstatutten — »vær venlig og høflig« — i ham. Han blinkede, blev rød, rejste sig og satte sig igen, kæmpende med sig selv for at gøre, hvad der for ham var det sværeste i livet — at sige noget ubehageligt til et menneske lige i ansigtet, at sige, hvad den anden, hvem det end var, ikke ventede. Han var så vant til at bøje sig for fyrst Vasilijs tone af afslappet selvtillid, at han følte, han ikke ville kunne modstå den nu, men han følte også, at det, han sagde nu, ville afgøre hans fremtid — om han ville følge den gamle vej eller den nye sti, som frimurerne så tillokkende havde vist ham, og hvor han fast troede, han ville blive genfødt til et nyt liv.
»Nå, min dreng,« sagde fyrst Vasilij spøgefuldt, »sig 'ja', så skriver jeg selv til hende, og vi slagter den fede kalv.«
Men før fyrst Vasilij havde sagt sin spøgefulde sætning færdig, mumlede Pierre, uden at se på ham og med en slags raseri, der fik ham til at ligne sin far, hviskende:
»Fyrste, jeg har ikke bedt Dem komme. Gå, vær så venlig — gå!« Og han sprang op og lukkede døren op for ham.
»Gå!« gentog han, forbavset over sig selv og glad over at se det udtryk af forvirring og frygt, der viste sig i fyrst Vasilijs ansigt.
»Hvad fejler De? Er De syg?«
»Gå!« gentog den skælvende stemme. Og fyrst Vasilij måtte gå uden at få nogen forklaring.

En uge senere tog Pierre afsked med sine nye venner, frimurerne, og efterlod store pengebeløb til almisser, og rejste til sine godser. Hans nye brødre gav ham breve med til frimurerne i Kiev og Odessa og lovede at skrive til ham og vejlede ham i hans nye virke.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The day after his initiation into the Lodge, Pierre sat at home reading a book and trying to understand the significance of the Square, one side of which symbolized God, another moral things, a third physical things, and the fourth a combination of these. Now and then his attention drifted from the book and the Square, and he found himself imagining a new plan for his life. At the Lodge the previous evening, he had heard that rumors of his duel had reached the Emperor, and that it would be wise for him to leave Petersburg. Pierre planned to go to his southern estates and attend to the welfare of his serfs. He was happily envisioning this new life when Prince Vasili suddenly walked into the room.

"My dear fellow, what have you been up to in Moscow? Why have you fallen out with Helene, mon cher? You're mistaken," said Prince Vasili as he entered. "I know all about it, and I can tell you with certainty that Helene is as innocent before you as Christ was before the Jews."
Pierre was about to reply, but Prince Vasili cut him off.

"And why didn't you simply come straight to me, as a friend? I know everything and I understand it all," he said. "You acted as a man of honor should — perhaps too hastily, but let's not get into that. But think of the position in which you're placing her and me in the eyes of society, and even of the court," he added, lowering his voice. "She's living in Moscow and you're here. Remember, dear boy" — and he pulled Pierre's arm down — "it's simply a misunderstanding. I'm sure you feel that yourself. Let's write her a letter right now, and she'll come here and everything will be cleared up — otherwise, my dear boy, I must warn you that you'll likely have to pay the consequences."
Prince Vasili gave Pierre a meaningful look.
"I know from reliable sources that the Dowager Empress is taking a keen interest in the whole affair. You know how fond she is of Helene."

Pierre tried several times to speak, but on one hand Prince Vasili wouldn't let him get a word in, and on the other, Pierre himself was afraid to begin speaking in the tone of firm refusal and disagreement he had resolved to use with his father-in-law. Moreover, the words of the Masonic statutes — "be kind and courteous" — kept echoing in his mind. He blinked, went red, got up, sat down again, struggling to do the hardest thing in the world for him — to say something unpleasant to someone's face, to say what the other person didn't expect. He was so accustomed to submitting to Prince Vasili's breezy self-assurance that he felt he would be unable to resist it now; yet he also felt that everything depended on what he said at this moment — whether he would go on in the same old rut or take that new path so attractively shown him by the Masons, on which he firmly believed he would be reborn.
"Now, dear boy," said Prince Vasili playfully, "just say 'yes,' and I'll write to her myself, and we'll kill the fatted calf."
But before Prince Vasili could finish his playful speech, Pierre — without looking at him, and with a kind of fury that made him resemble his father — muttered in a whisper:
"Prince, I did not invite you here. Go. Please go!" And he jumped up and opened the door for him.
"Go!" he repeated, astonished at himself and glad to see the look of confusion and fear on Prince Vasili's face.
"What's the matter with you? Are you ill?"
"Go!" the trembling voice repeated. And Prince Vasili had to leave without any explanation.

A week later, Pierre, having said goodbye to his new friends the Masons and leaving large sums of money with them for charitable works, departed for his estates. His new brothers gave him letters of introduction to the Kiev and Odessa Masons and promised to write to him and guide him in his new endeavors.
